content: Pre-medical education, often referred to as pre-med, is a specific academic and extracurricular track pursued by undergraduate students in the United States who intend to apply to medical school. Pre-Med Timeline During their first year of college, pre-med students typically organize their academic schedules to include the prerequisite courses required for medical school admission. After completing at least one semester, many students begin engaging in extracurricular activities that demonstrate their dedication to the field of medicine, such as volunteering in healthcare settings or participating in research projects. By their junior year, most pre-med students register for and take the Medical College Admission Test (MCAT), a standardized exam that medical schools use to evaluate applicants' qualifications. Following the MCAT, students apply to medical schools through the American Medical College Application Service (AMCAS) or, in the case of non-AMCAS schools, through the institution's individual application system. The application process involves a comprehensive review of the applicant's academic performance, extracurricular activities, work experience, and a personal statement. After submitting their primary application, students may receive secondary applications from individual medical schools. These secondary applications typically include essay questions that require thoughtful and specific responses. Applicants who meet the schools' criteria may then be invited for interviews, which are considered a significant milestone in the application process. Once the interviews are completed, the application process is finalized, and students await admission decisions from the schools to which they applied. Coursework The Association of American Medical Colleges (AAMC) has established a set of standard prerequisite courses that all pre-med students must complete. However, individual medical schools may impose additional requirements. Pre-medical coursework is not a formal major but rather a track that follows a specific curriculum. While many pre-med students choose to major in natural sciences such as biology, chemistry, or physics, this is not mandatory. Approximately 25% of medical school matriculants major in non-science fields, including anthropology, philosophy, or other humanities disciplines. The core courses required for pre-med students typically include: General Chemistry I and II, with laboratory components. General Biology I and II, with laboratory components (some schools may accept zoology as a substitute for the second semester of biology). Organic Chemistry I and II, with laboratory components (some schools may allow biochemistry to replace the second semester of organic chemistry). General Physics I and II, with laboratory components. One or two semesters of mathematics, usually including Calculus I and either Calculus II or a statistics course. English and writing courses. In addition to these foundational courses, pre-med students are often encouraged or required to take advanced biology and chemistry electives, such as cellular biology, biochemistry, physical chemistry, or genetics. The specific requirements for these advanced courses vary by institution. Pre-Medical Education in Other Countries In Australia, several universities offer threeor four-year undergraduate degrees in Medical Science or Biomedical Science. These programs are similar in content and purpose to pre-medical tracks in the United States, as they prepare students for entry into graduate medical schools. Many graduates of these programs aim to pursue further medical education at the graduate level.
